{{Short description|Combinatorial analog of the Borsuk-Ulam theorem}}
[[File:TuckerLemExample.png|thumb|350px|In this example, where n=2, the red 1-simplex has vertices which are labelled by the same number with opposite signs. Tucker's lemma states that for such a triangulation at least one such 1-simplex must exist.]]

In [[mathematics]], '''Tucker's lemma''' is a [[combinatorics|combinatorial]] analog of the [[Borsuk&ndash;Ulam theorem]], named after [[Albert W. Tucker]].

Let T be a [[Triangulation (topology)|triangulation]] of the closed ''n''-dimensional [[Ball (mathematics)|ball]] <math>B_n</math>. Assume T is antipodally symmetric on the boundary [[sphere]] <math>S_{n-1}</math>. That means that the subset of [[Simplex|simplices]] of T which are in <math>S_{n-1}</math> provides a triangulation of <math>S_{n-1}</math> where if σ is a simplex then so is −σ.
Let <math>L:V(T)\to\{+1,-1,+2,-2,...,+n,-n\}</math> be a labeling of the vertices of T which is an [[odd function]] on <math>S_{n-1}</math>, i.e., <math>L(-v) = -L(v)</math> for every vertex <math>v\in S_{n-1}</math>.
Then Tucker's lemma states that T contains a ''complementary edge'' - an edge (a 1-simplex) whose vertices are labelled by the same number but with opposite signs.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Matoušek | first = Jiří | author-link = Jiří Matoušek (mathematician)
 | isbn = 3-540-00362-2
 | pages = 34–45
 | publisher = [[Springer-Verlag]]
 | title = Using the Borsuk–Ulam Theorem
 | title-link = Using the Borsuk–Ulam Theorem
 | year = 2003}}</ref>

== Proofs ==
The first proofs were non-constructive, by way of contradiction.<ref>{{citation | last = Tucker | first = Albert W. | author-link = Albert W. Tucker | contribution = Some topological properties of disk and sphere | location = Toronto | mr = 0020254 | pages = 285–309 | publisher = [[University of Toronto Press]] | title = Proc. First Canadian Math. Congress, Montreal, 1945 | year = 1946}}</ref>

Later, constructive proofs were found, which also supplied algorithms for finding the complementary edge.<ref>{{citation | last1 = Freund | first1 = Robert M. | last2 = Todd | first2 = Michael J. | doi = 10.1016/0097-3165(81)90027-3 | issue = 3 | journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | mr = 618536 | pages = 321–325 | series = Series A | title = A constructive proof of Tucker's combinatorial lemma | volume = 30 | year = 1981| doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{citation | last1 = Freund | first1 = Robert M. | last2 = Todd | first2 = Michael J. | title = A constructive proof of Tucker's combinatorial lemma | year = 1980|url=http://oai.dtic.mil/oai/oai?verb=getRecord&metadataPrefix=html&identifier=ADA090797|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150622120050/http://oai.dtic.mil/oai/oai?verb=getRecord&metadataPrefix=html&identifier=ADA090797|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 22, 2015}}</ref> Basically, the algorithms are path-based: they start at a certain point or edge of the triangulation, then go from simplex to simplex according to prescribed rules, until it is not possible to proceed any more. It can be proved that the path must end in a simplex which contains a complementary edge.

An easier proof of Tucker's lemma uses the more general [[Ky Fan lemma]], which has a simple algorithmic proof.

The following description illustrates the algorithm for <math>n=2</math>.<ref name="Meunier10">{{citation | url=http://pretty.structures.free.fr/talks/Meunier.pdf | title=Sperner and Tucker lemmas | publisher=Algorithms and Pretty Theorems Blog | date=2010 | accessdate=25 May 2015 | author=Meunier, Frédéric | pages=46–64}}</ref> Note that in this case <math>B_n</math> is a disk and there are 4 possible labels: <math>-2, -1, 1, 2</math>, like the figure at the top-right.

Start outside the ball and consider the labels of the boundary vertices. Because the labeling is an odd function on the boundary, the boundary must have both positive and negative labels:
* If the boundary contains only <math>\pm 1</math> or only <math>\pm 2</math>, there must be a complementary edge on the boundary. Done.
* Otherwise, the boundary must contain <math>(+1,-2)</math> edges. Moreover, the number of <math>(+1,-2)</math> edges on the boundary must be odd.

Select an <math>(+1,-2)</math> edge and go through it. There are three cases:
* You are now in a <math>(+1,-2,+2)</math> simplex. Done.
* You are now in a <math>(+1,-2,-1)</math> simplex. Done.
* You are in a simplex with another <math>(+1,-2)</math> edge. Go through it and continue.

The last case can take you outside the ball. However, since the number of <math>(+1,-2)</math> edges on the boundary must be odd, there must be a new, unvisited <math>(+1,-2)</math> edge on the boundary. Go through it and continue.

This walk must end inside the ball, either in a <math>(+1,-2,+2)</math> or in a <math>(+1,-2,-1)</math> simplex. Done.

== Run-time ==
The run-time of the algorithm described above is polynomial in the triangulation size. This is considered bad, since the triangulations might be very large. It would be desirable to find an algorithm which is logarithmic in the triangulation size. However, the problem of finding a complementary edge is [[PPA (complexity)|PPA]]-complete even for <math>n=2</math> dimensions. This implies that there is not too much hope for finding a fast algorithm.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Aisenberg | first1 = James
 | last2 = Bonet | first2 = Maria Luisa | author2-link = María Luisa Bonet
 | last3 = Buss | first3 = Sam | author3-link = Samuel Buss
 | id = {{ECCC|2015|15|163}}
 | title = 2-D Tucker is PPA complete
 | year = 2015}}</ref>
